newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICA SEEKS TO GUARD PATAGONIAN TOOTHFISH.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICA SEEKS TO GUARD PATAGONIAN TOOTHFISH.

text.p: South Africa's air force and navy have been recruited in the fight to protect the country's remote Patagonian toothfish resource, Tourism and Environment Affairs Minister Pallo Jordan said on Tuesday.

Jordan, who has responsibility for sea fisheries, said in a speech to parliament that the toothfish fishery, based around the Prince Edward Islands halfway between South Africa and the Antarctic, posed a great law enforcement challenge.
He said the air force and navy were helping to patrol the area, just within South Africa's 200-mile exclusive economic zone.

Patagonian toothfish expert Martin Purves told Reuters the fishery off the Prince Edward Islands had been discovered only at the beginning of 1996 and had quickly lured foreign long- line ships which were experiencing declining catches in established fisheries off the South American coast.
"It's a very valuable fishery. It's an export species that goes to markets in the East and America," Purves said.

"It's more valuable than most of the commercial species you find off-shore from South Africa so there's a lot of international interest. There's been reports of up to 60 vessels being involved since the middle of last year."
Purves said the Patagonian toothfish was vulnerable to over-fishing because it took a long time to mature sexually, growing to more than two metres in length and 100 kg in weight.
"Once you start over-exploiting it, it takes quite a while before it recovers," he said.
"It's a valuable resource for South Africa to protect... A lot of operators have gone in there and have been fishing illegally."
Purves said the fishery extended beyond South Africa's economic zone into Antarctic waters, but South Africa had been given responsibility for managing it under terms of an international treaty.
He said attempts had been made to control toothfish-fishing vessels by requiring them to install satellite tracking devices, but many of the ships simply turned the devices off.
